value.overview: The Tody Motmot is the smallest member of the motmot family and the only species in the genus Hylomanes. It is a quiet, compact forest bird with green upperparts, a rufous-brown head and neck, a dark facial mask, pale underparts, and a short tail without the long racket tips seen in many other motmots. It usually stays in dense, shaded vegetation and is more often heard or glimpsed briefly than observed in the open.
value.classification: The Tody Motmot belongs to the motmot family, Momotidae, in the order Coraciiformes. It is the sole species in the genus Hylomanes.
value.identification: This small motmot is about 16–17 cm long. Adults have green upperparts, a brownish or rufous head and neck, a blue line or spot above the eye, a blackish facial mask, and a pale throat and belly. The breast is often greenish or grayish with fine streaking. Its short, rounded tail lacks the conspicuous racket tips of larger motmots. In Costa Rica, birds may appear duller, with less white on the throat and less blue above the eye.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southern Mexico through Central America to Colombia and adjacent parts of northwestern South America. In Costa Rica it is a very uncommon, localized resident, especially associated with humid evergreen forest on the Pacific side of the Cordillera de Guanacaste, generally at about 500–1,000 m. It has also been recorded in foothill forest on the Caribbean slope, including the Tilarán Mountains and areas near Bijagua. It favors dark understory, ravines, streamside vegetation, and relatively undisturbed forest.
value.migrationStatus: The Tody Motmot is considered sedentary and has no known regular migration. In Costa Rica it is a year-round resident; reported local movements are not thought to represent long-distance migration.
value.breeding: Breeding information is limited. The species excavates a small tunnel or burrow in soft soil, apparently often in an earthen bank or on the forest floor. Adults have been observed with recently fledged young in late spring and early summer in parts of Central America, and a recently fledged juvenile was recorded in Costa Rica in late May. Details of courtship, clutch size, incubation, and parental care remain incompletely documented.
value.dietFeeding: The Tody Motmot feeds mainly on insects and other arthropods, including beetles, butterflies, dragonflies, spiders, and other small invertebrates. It may also take small vertebrates such as lizards and consume occasional fruit. It commonly waits quietly on a low perch in the understory before making a short downward or outward flight to seize prey from vegetation, leaf litter, or the ground.
value.behavior: Usually solitary or found in pairs, the Tody Motmot is secretive and spends much of its time perched quietly in dense, shaded understory. It may forage along ravines, stream edges, and forest-floor tangles. Its small size, subdued movements, and preference for dark forest make it difficult to detect. It is generally less conspicuous than larger motmots and often remains still when approached.

conservation.populationTrend: A reliable current global population trend is not clearly documented. The species remains relatively uncommon and localized in parts of its range, including Costa Rica, but is not currently considered globally threatened.
